I don't have many stories that I can classify as really creepy, but I wanted to post one of my grandma's to help encourage other posters :)

This story occurs in the 1970's. My grandma, dad, and his brother were all asleep. My grandpa worked nights in a hospital and wouldn't come home until ~7am.

My grandma woke up to what sounded like a door banging open. She assumed it was one of her kids going to the bathroom or into the kitchen for water. She fell back asleep, and didn't wake up again until she heard her bedroom door slowly creak open. The light in the hallway was on, and when she opened her eyes she saw the black outline of a man standing right above her in bed. She screamed (naturally) and the man booked it out of the front door.

The cops were called, but unfortunately the man was never caught. My dad and uncle slept throughout the whole thing, and only woke up after my grandma ran in to check on them. The only thing that was taken was $50 that was left on the kitchen table. They believe he got in through an unlocked door (my grandma explained that life was different back than, and they lived in a trusting neighborhood).

So unknown robber, let's never meet. But thanks I guess for making me paranoid about locking doors.

Self-Driving Cars May End the Fines That Fill City Coffers

I know all cities/towns do this. It's politically easy tax money for them. None of their constituents will complain about fines for law breakers. That doesn't make it a good idea though.

It creates a situation where the local government becomes dependent on law breakers. Does any municipality morally want to be in that position? It's sets up some twisted incentives for governments.
Once that happens, they're going to start raising the other fines and taxes through the roof.. as well as invent new ones.

The bigger question is will people willing buy vehicles that know everywhere you go, how long you're there, and possibly what you do or bring into the vehicle, and has the ability to report that information to anyone with access to the programing?

The day I can afford a self driving car, I'm going to whore that thing out to everyone I know for gas money. Need a lift?, I'll send the car, leave gas money in the glove box. Good luck tracking anyone where anyone can start a cab service.

in a scenario where a self driving cab becomes an accessible option, I am sure the cities will raise more money from property tax from all the parking lots scattered all over (currently these places get tax exemptions) then they lose from these taxes.Cites could also save by letting go some of the parking staff ... And if the self driving car provides a more affordable transportation to some people, I believe, the city will raise more money from income taxes (although some of this is federal), by allowing people to easier access jobs and an over all better allocation of workers more in tune with the geographical location that the people can afford and the location they are needed.
Maybe relying on people screwing up is a bad business model...

The alternative is for the councils to invest in the cars themselves then charge enough for usage to cover the lost revenue. Communal cars is where the greatest societal benefit for autonomous cars comes from anyway.
